scenes.visual: Title card 'The Few That Survive' on the same warm cream background and flat cartoon style as the first film, no molecular structures. Colour map carried over: microbes, here the SENSITIVE bacteria, = TEAL circles (as in the first film and the lesson's simulation); GOLD = whatever attacks microbes, here the antibiotic's hit marks (as in the lesson's figure). New for this film: RESISTANT bacteria = ORANGE rounded squares (as in the simulation's key); YOUR CELL = a large pale-pink cartoon cell; VIRUS = tiny purple particles. A DAY COUNTER box sits top right, as in the first film, labelled 'schematic'. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The first film raced microbes against the body's own defenses, but an antibiotic attacks the microbes directly. If it kills almost every bacterium, how can the infection come back? To answer that, start with what the drug needs.
scenes.visual: A small replay of the first film's race view (TEAL curve, GOLD defense bar) shrinks into a corner. A pill bottle labelled 'antibiotic' rolls in and aims at a crowd of TEAL circles. Most of the circles vanish; a question mark hangs over the few left: 'how can it come back?'
scenes.narration: The first film raced microbes against the body's own defenses, but an antibiotic attacks the microbes directly. If it kills almost every bacterium, how can the infection come back? To answer that, start with what the drug needs.

scenes.tts: An antibiotic is a drug that kills bacteria or stops them growing and dividing. To work, it needs something to hit. Many antibiotics block the building of the bacterial cell wall. Others jam bacterial ribosomes, so the cell cannot make proteins.
scenes.visual: One rod-shaped TEAL bacterium fills the left of the screen, its thick outer cell wall and small dot-like ribosomes labelled. GOLD block marks land on the wall ('wall building blocked') and on the ribosomes ('ribosomes jammed'). The bacterium stops and fades. Same layout as the lesson's figure 'What antibiotics hit'.
scenes.narration: An antibiotic is a drug that kills bacteria or stops them growing and dividing. To work, it needs something to hit. Many antibiotics block the building of the bacterial cell wall. Others jam bacterial ribosomes, so the cell cannot make proteins.

scenes.tts: Now look at a virus. It has no cell wall and no ribosomes of its own. It works inside one of your cells and uses that cell's ribosomes. These drugs find no bacterial part there to hit. So antibiotics do not treat colds or flu.
scenes.visual: On the right, a large pale-pink cell labelled 'your cell' with a thin membrane and its own ribosomes; tiny purple 'virus' particles sit inside. GOLD marks fly toward it and pass by, finding no cell wall or bacterial ribosome to land on. A crossed-out tag reads 'colds, flu: no bacterial target'.
scenes.narration: Now look at a virus. It has no cell wall and no ribosomes of its own. It works inside one of your cells and uses that cell's ribosomes. These drugs find no bacterial part there to hit. So antibiotics do not treat colds or flu.

scenes.tts: Back to bacteria, now a large population of them in an infection. Most are sensitive, which means the drug kills or stops them. But a few may already carry a gene that lets them survive the drug. These are resistant.
scenes.visual: Zoom out to a dish-like field crowded with TEAL circles labelled 'sensitive'. Scattered among them are a handful of ORANGE rounded squares labelled 'resistant: carry a survival gene (already there)'. The DAY COUNTER reads 'day 0'. No counts are shown.
scenes.narration: Back to bacteria, now a large population of them in an infection. Most are sensitive, which means the drug kills or stops them. But a few may already carry a gene that lets them survive the drug. These are resistant.

scenes.tts: Antibiotic resistance is the ability of some bacteria to survive a drug that kills others of their kind. Start the drug. Here it kills the sensitive cells. Round after round, the teal cells disappear. The orange ones survive, because they resist the drug.
scenes.visual: GOLD marks sweep across the field in waves while the DAY COUNTER ticks. TEAL circles turn to dashed empty outlines and vanish wave by wave. GOLD marks also land on the ORANGE squares but fade without effect; a small tag reads 'resists the drug'. A label: 'schematic, a drug that kills'.
scenes.narration: Antibiotic resistance is the ability of some bacteria to survive a drug that kills others of their kind. Start the drug. Here it kills the sensitive cells. Round after round, the teal cells disappear. The orange ones survive, because they resist the drug.

scenes.tts: Now every teal cell is gone. Only the few orange cells remain, with empty space around them. When this population grows back, what will it be made of?
scenes.visual: The field is nearly empty: dashed outlines where TEAL cells were, and the few ORANGE squares. A prompt reads 'when it grows back, what will it be made of?'
scenes.narration: Now every teal cell is gone. Only the few orange cells remain, with empty space around them. When this population grows back, what will it be made of?

scenes.visual: Hold the nearly empty field and the prompt with a small countdown ring. Nothing moves.

scenes.tts: Resistant cells. With their competition gone, the orange cells divide and fill the space. The drug did not create them. In this example, they were there before the drug. It removed their competition.
scenes.visual: The ORANGE squares divide, two, then four, then more, spreading outward until the field is full again and entirely ORANGE. The DAY COUNTER keeps ticking (schematic). A tag pins to one square: 'there before the drug'.
scenes.narration: Resistant cells. With their competition gone, the orange cells divide and fill the space. The drug did not create them. In this example, they were there before the drug. It removed their competition.

scenes.tts: This is natural selection: individuals with a helpful trait survive and reproduce more. Here the trait is resistance, and the drug did the selecting. The bacteria did not choose to change. And the person did not become resistant. The bacteria did.
scenes.visual: A banner 'natural selection' over the all-ORANGE field. Beside it a cartoon person outline with a tag 'not resistant', crossed check, and an arrow from the field to the word 'bacteria' with a tick. The bacteria choose nothing: a small tag reads 'no choice, just survivors'.
scenes.narration: This is natural selection: individuals with a helpful trait survive and reproduce more. Here the trait is resistance, and the drug did the selecting. The bacteria did not choose to change. And the person did not become resistant. The bacteria did.

scenes.tts: There is one more route. A resistant bacterium can pass a resistance gene to another bacterium. That neighbour now survives the drug too. So resistance can spread to bacteria that never met the drug.
scenes.visual: Two cells touch: an ORANGE square passes a small DNA ring labelled 'plasmid carrying a resistance gene' to a TEAL circle beside it. The TEAL circle uses the gene and turns into an ORANGE square, now resistant to that drug. Off to the side, a second ring passes on to a cell that never saw a GOLD mark.
scenes.narration: There is one more route. A resistant bacterium can pass a resistance gene to another bacterium. That neighbour now survives the drug too. So resistance can spread to bacteria that never met the drug.

scenes.tts: Killing almost every bacterium is not a cure if resistant survivors grow back. Using an antibiotic can favor any resistant bacteria present. An antibiotic spares resistant bacteria, and the survivors can take over.
scenes.visual: A row of three mini fields, left to right: mixed TEAL and ORANGE, then GOLD sweep, then all ORANGE (schematic). The line 'An antibiotic spares resistant bacteria, and the survivors can take over.' types out across the bottom.
scenes.narration: Killing almost every bacterium is not a cure if resistant survivors grow back. Using an antibiotic can favor any resistant bacteria present. An antibiotic spares resistant bacteria, and the survivors can take over.

scenes.visual: End card: the Hex mascot beside one ORANGE square, with the line 'An antibiotic spares resistant bacteria, and the survivors can take over.' A thin GOLD bar runs under the text.
